title: They’re building an open-source backup of Twitter
summary:
The killer line in this whole saga is basically: Twitter’s broken, the API is hostile, so the users are just… rebuilding access themselves. @exgenesis launches “Community Archive” as a public database + API where people voluntarily upload their own Twitter archives (with privacy reassurances like “processed locally, only minimal data leaves your machine”). The pitch lands because everyone has the same pain story—@ultimape is the poster child, spiraling from “Can’t use search now” to “I literally can't post links off site anymore” to “Why is twitter so broken?” and then immediately going “So cool” and uploading 122,086 tweets.

What triggered the wave was @exgenesis’s viral explainer video (the kitchen/egg clip) and then aggressive-but-playful social proof: he starts tagging “people I would be EXCITED if they uploaded their archives” (@visakanv, @gwern, @Aella_Girl, @nickcammarata, etc.), which turns archiving into a status move. Momentum peaks as builders show off quick wins: @_ceee_ makes a “tweet frequency by hour” chart, @DefenderOfBasic riffs that into an idea for “circadian rhythm matching,” and the project hits Hacker News with 1.16M tweets logged. Meanwhile, the community keeps hitting platform friction (people getting asked for driver’s licenses, archive downloads breaking), which only reinforces the core argument: you can’t rely on X to let you access your own history.

Then it graduates from “cool workaround” to “real ecosystem” with the Feb 2025 NYC hackathon (@exgenesis + @DefenderOfBasic). The peak outputs are wonderfully unhinged and genuinely useful: @IvanVendrov wins 1st prize for “meme contagion dynamics” that names “patient zeros” for viral tokens like “covid,” “chatgpt,” and “tpot,” while @emergentvibe cranks out a social graph viz and semantic correlation plots (“people are happy when they are traveling”). The arc doesn’t die after the event—@exgenesis publishes a hackathon report citing ~16M tweets from ~200+ people, and months later @univrsw3th4rt is still uploading 40K tweets—so it’s become a durable counter-infrastructure. Why care? Because it’s a live experiment in data sovereignty: a niche Twitter subculture is turning personal archives into shared, buildable public memory—plus a playground for analytics, search, and memetics research that X itself has priced out.
